candidates.attacker_control: The full encoded JWT string is attacker-controlled in typical use (HTTP Authorization header, cookie, or request parameter), as illustrated by the README decode examples (`JWT.getDecoder().decode(encodedJWT, verifier)`). The attacker fully controls the header segment (including the claimed `alg`), the payload segment (including `sub`, `iss`, `exp`, and custom claims), and can append the trailing dot that selects the unverified two-segment path.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Considered that unsecured JWTs are an intentional feature (`UnsecuredSigner`, README lists `none`), but the code comments state the unsecured form should be accepted only when `alg == none` and no verifiers were provided; the two-segment path defeats that condition, so this is not the intended behavior. Verified there is no other guard: `getParts` is the only parse point and is called only from the two public decode methods (relation index + text search); the private decode contains no `algorithm == none` requirement; the encoder always produces three segments so this input cannot arise from normal encoding. Checked that `String.split` removes trailing empty strings, which is why the two-part array plus the `endsWith(".")` check is the enabling condition. No test sources exist in the snapshot to demonstrate intended behavior, and the code was not executed.
candidates.impact: Complete bypass of JWT signature verification: an unauthenticated attacker can forge a token with arbitrary `sub`/`iss`/`exp`/custom claims that applications using this library will treat as authentic, enabling authentication and authorization bypass (e.g., impersonating any subject or escalating roles/claims) wherever the library is the token-validation boundary. With no verifiers configured the same two-part form is accepted for any algorithm; with verifiers configured the signature is still never checked.
candidates.prerequisites: Application decodes a JWT with `JWTDecoder.decode` (either the `Verifier...` overload or the `Map`/`keyFunction` overload) as documented. No special configuration is required: the bypass occurs whether verifiers are supplied or not; with verifiers supplied, `canVerify` merely determines whether a verifier object is selected, which is irrelevant because `verifier.verify(...)` is never invoked for `parts.length == 2`. The payload must be valid base64url-encoded JSON deserializable into `JWT`, and any `exp`/`nbf` claims the attacker includes must pass the local clock checks (the attacker can set these freely or omit them).
candidates.root_cause: `JWTDecoder.getParts` accepts a two-segment token when `encodedJWT.endsWith(".")` (lines 174-182), but the private `decode` gates both the missing-verifier check and the actual `verifier.verify()` call on `parts.length == 3` (lines 149-157). No code requires `header.algorithm == Algorithm.none` for the two-segment form. The public methods only special-case the unsigned form with the condition `header.algorithm == none && parts.length == 2 && (verifiers empty)` (lines 69 and 119); when that condition is false (e.g., alg=HS256, or any alg with a verifier supplied), execution falls through to the private decode where a two-segment token skips verification entirely and the payload is deserialized (line 159).
candidates.title: JWT signature verification bypass for trailing-dot two-segment tokens in JWTDecoder
candidates.trace: 1) `decode(String, Verifier...)` (line 60) or `decode(String, Map, Function)` (line 112) calls `getParts(encodedJWT)` (lines 65/116). 2) `getParts` splits on `.` and returns a two-element array for any string ending in `.` (`String.split` drops the trailing empty segment), satisfying `parts.length == 2 && encodedJWT.endsWith(".")` (line 177). 3) The unsecured fast path at line 69/119 is skipped because the header's `alg` is a real algorithm (e.g., HS256/RS256) or because verifiers were provided. 4) A verifier may be selected via `canVerify` (lines 74-79 / 124-130), but in the private `decode` the missing-verifier exception (line 149) and the `verifier.verify(header.algorithm, message, signature)` call (lines 153-157) both require `parts.length == 3`; with two parts neither executes. 5) The payload is deserialized at line 159 and returned after only expiration/not-before checks, so unsigned, attacker-chosen claims are accepted as a verified result. (Source-level reasoning only; not executed.)
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed (no code/tests executed per review constraints). The exact behavior of `String.split` trailing-empty removal and the concrete end-to-end call path were derived from source semantics, not execution. Library consumers' own token-format pre-validation (outside this repository) is unknown and could incidentally reject trailing-dot strings.
candidates.weakness_type: Missing signature verification / improper verification of cryptographic signature (authentication bypass)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 35 model-visible files (34 Java files under src/main/java/org/primeframework/jwt plus pom.xml, README.md, .gitignore); no test sources, no other modules. Files read: JWTDecoder, JWTEncoder, JWTUtils, OpenIDConnect, Signer, UnsecuredSigner, Verifier, HMACSigner/HMACVerifier, RSASigner/RSAVerifier/RSAUtils/PEMUtils, Mapper/JacksonModule/ZonedDateTime(De)Serializer, JWT/Header/Algorithm and the remaining domain classes, README, pom.xml. Relation index reported complete coverage (35/35 source files indexed, 0 missing, no build/test execution, no SAST oracle); index was used only for navigation and every relied-upon edge was verified in source text. The finding's root cause was traced across getParts, both public decode overloads, and the private decode method; the signature-verification gap is self-contained in JWTDecoder.java.
limitations: Static, source-only review; no code, tests, or scanners were executed, so the bypass is not runtime-confirmed.
No test sources exist in the snapshot, so intended behavior is inferred from Javadoc/comments, README examples, and code structure.

Consumer-side preprocessing of token strings (e.g., rejecting inputs ending in '.') is outside this repository and unknown; such a filter would mitigate the issue for those callers but is not part of the library API contract.

The relation index provides syntactic navigation only (no data-flow/reachability proof) and did not model library consumers outside this repository; impact assessment for consuming applications is therefore an inference.
Dependency-level issues (Jackson 2.8.1) were not investigated against external advisories, per review constraints.

rejected_leads.lead: OpenIDConnect.c_hash computes 256 left-most bits (full SHA-256 digest) instead of the spec's 128-bit left half
rejected_leads.reason: Spec-compliance/interoperability defect: a relying party computing the standard c_hash would reject a mismatching value, which produces a functional failure rather than a demonstrated authentication bypass. Not selected as it does not meet the strongest-impact threshold and is not clearly attacker-exploitable within this library.

rejected_leads.lead: JWT claim getters (getBoolean/getInteger/getLong/getList) perform unchecked casts and parsing, and ZonedDateTimeDeserializer can propagate DateTimeException for extreme epoch values
rejected_leads.reason: Could cause application-level exceptions (potential DoS) when callers use these helpers on attacker-supplied claims, but there is no evidence of a security-boundary bypass or privilege gain, and misuse depends on the consuming application.

rejected_leads.lead: Verifier selection loop in decode(String, Verifier...) keeps the last matching verifier rather than the first, contrary to the Javadoc
rejected_leads.reason: Selection is by algorithm capability only and callers normally supply a single verifier; no concrete security impact identified from this mismatch alone.

rejected_leads.lead: RSAUtils/PEMUtils index-based PEM extraction can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when a suffix appears before a prefix
rejected_leads.reason: Inputs are operator-supplied key material (not remote attacker input in-library), and the impact is a startup/exception failure, so it is not a stronger candidate than the decoder bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: Map-based decode accepts an `alg=none` token when the verifier map is empty (line 119); stale Jackson 2.8.1 dependency in pom.xml
rejected_leads.reason: The empty-map acceptance appears intentional per the in-code comment and is a related, weaker manifestation of the same unsecured-acceptance root cause (not split into a second candidate). The dependency version was not pursued because external CVE/database lookups were out of scope and no source-level exploit chain was traced.

summary: The repository is the `com.inversoft:prime-jwt` library (34 Java sources under src/main/java, plus pom.xml/README/.gitignore; no test sources). Review focused on the decode/verify path. One strong source-level candidate: JWT signature-verification bypass in `JWTDecoder` for two-segment encoded JWTs ending in a dot. `getParts` explicitly accepts `parts.length == 2 && encodedJWT.endsWith(".")` as the unsigned (unsecured) JWT form, but the downstream private `decode` only enforces verifier presence and performs `verifier.verify(...)` when `parts.length == 3`. Nothing in that path requires the header algorithm to be `none`, and nothing rejects a two-segment token whose header claims HS*/RS*. Consequently a caller-supplied string of the form `<header-segment>.<payload-segment>.` is deserialized as a JWT with no signature check, even when the caller passed a matching HMAC/RSA verifier (and even when zero verifiers are passed, since the `MissingVerifierException` check is likewise guarded by `parts.length == 3`). This defeats the documented intent in the comments ("If the JWT is signed or any verifiers were provided don't do it") and allows forged claims to be accepted by applications using the library's primary decode API. Secondary observations (OIDC `c_hash` bit-length deviation, unchecked casts in JWT claim getters, last-match verifier selection, PEM index handling) were examined but are not submitted.
